pathologies.module: MODULE 1 - SINUS RHYTHMS & SINUS NODE DISORDERS
pathologies.definition: The normal rhythm of the heart. The sinoatrial (SA) node starts every beat at 60-100 bpm and the impulse travels normally through the atria, AV node and ventricles. It is the standard against which every other rhythm is compared.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 60-100 bpm
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Upright in lead II, uniform, one P before every QRS
PR interval: 0.12-0.20 s, constant
QRS complex: Narrow (< 0.12 s)
R-R interval: Constant (very slight variation is normal)
ST segment: Isoelectric (flat)
Other relevant characteristics: P wave is upright in lead II and inverted in aVR; every P is followed by a QRS and a T wave.
simulation_parameters: P-wave behavior: Present, uniform, upright, 1:1 with every QRS
Other: PR about 0.16 s; upright T wave; very slight baseline wander for realism.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: None. The patient has a regular pulse, normal blood pressure and adequate perfusion. Any symptoms are due to a cause other than the rhythm (pain, fever, anemia, sepsis, hypoxia).
pathologies.diagnosis: Rhythm strip or 12-lead ECG that meets ALL criteria: regular rhythm, rate 60-100, upright P before each QRS, PR 0.12-0.20 s and QRS < 0.12 s. Use the systematic sequence: rate, rhythm, P wave, PR interval, QRS.
pathologies.treatment: No antiarrhythmic treatment is needed. If the patient is unwell, look for non-cardiac causes (hypoxia, hypoglycemia, sepsis, hypovolemia). Remember: an organized rhythm on the monitor with NO pulse is pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and needs CPR.
pathologies.recommendations: Always correlate the monitor with the patient: check pulse, blood pressure, skin and mental status. Use this rhythm as your reference every time you interpret another strip.
key_learning_points: Every QRS has a matching upright P wave in lead II.
Regular, 60-100 bpm, PR 0.12-0.20 s, QRS narrow.
A normal-looking rhythm on the monitor does not guarantee a pulse: check the patient.
sources: 1. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Normal sinus rhythm. litfl.com/ecg-library
2. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 5: Sinus Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/5-sinus-rhythms

required.explanation: Normal sinus P-wave morphology.
Each P wave conducts to a QRS.

supporting.explanation: Rate in the normal sinus range.
Regular R-R intervals.
PR interval is normal and constant.
QRS is narrow.
No premature beat pattern.
No pacing spikes.

conflicts.explanation: Non-sinus P-wave pattern conflicts with NSR.
Irregularly irregular rhythm conflicts with NSR.

pathologies.module: MODULE 1 - SINUS RHYTHMS & SINUS NODE DISORDERS
pathologies.definition: A sinus rhythm with a rate below 60 bpm. The SA node is still the pacemaker and conduction is normal, but it fires slowly. It can be normal (athletes, sleep) or a sign of disease.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: < 60 bpm (typically 40-59)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Normal, upright, one before each QRS
PR interval: 0.12-0.20 s, constant
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Constant but long (> 1 s)
ST segment: Isoelectric
Other relevant characteristics: Same appearance as sinus rhythm with a longer pause between the T wave and the next P wave.
simulation_parameters: Other: Slightly more prominent T wave; long isoelectric segment before each P.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Often none. When symptomatic: dizziness, fatigue, near-syncope or syncope, shortness of breath, chest pain, confusion, hypotension, and signs of shock or acute heart failure.
pathologies.diagnosis: Sinus criteria with a rate below 60. Look for the cause: athletic conditioning, sleep, high vagal tone, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, raised intracranial pressure, inferior MI, sick sinus syndrome. Then decide whether the patient is stable or unstable.
pathologies.treatment: Asymptomatic: no treatment, treat the cause. Symptomatic or unstable (hypotension, acute altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure): atropine 1 mg IV bolus, repeat every 3-5 min (maximum 3 mg). If atropine fails: transcutaneous pacing, or dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min, or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min. Prepare for transvenous pacing and consult cardiology.
pathologies.recommendations: Review medications, check oxygenation, electrolytes and thyroid function. Keep pacing pads ready if the rate is falling. Atropine is unlikely to work in a transplanted (denervated) heart: go straight to pacing or catecholamines.
key_learning_points: It is sinus rhythm, only slower: rate below 60 bpm.
Treat the patient, not the number: only symptomatic bradycardia needs atropine or pacing.
Atropine 1 mg IV, repeat every 3-5 min, maximum 3 mg.
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.

required.explanation: Sinus bradycardia is below 60 bpm.
Sinus P-wave morphology is preserved.
Each P conducts to QRS.

supporting.explanation: Regular rhythm.
PR is normal and constant.
QRS is narrow.
No ectopic premature beat pattern.

conflicts.explanation: A rate at or above 60 bpm conflicts with sinus bradycardia.
Pacing activity argues for a paced rhythm.

pathologies.module: MODULE 1 - SINUS RHYTHMS & SINUS NODE DISORDERS
pathologies.definition: A sinus rhythm with a rate above 100 bpm. It is almost always the body's response to something (fever, pain, anxiety, blood loss, hypoxia) and not a primary heart disease.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 101-150 bpm (maximum roughly 220 minus age)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Normal and upright; may merge with the T wave of the previous beat at faster rates
PR interval: 0.12-0.20 s (tends to shorten)
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Constant and short
ST segment: May show mild rate-related depression
Other relevant characteristics: Gradual onset and gradual slowing (unlike SVT, which starts and stops abruptly). Rate rarely exceeds 150-160 at rest in adults.
simulation_parameters: P-wave behavior: Present and upright; approaches the previous T wave as rate increases
Other: Shorter T wave and PR interval at faster rates.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Palpitations, anxiety, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, plus the signs of the cause: fever, pain, pallor or bleeding, dehydration, low oxygen saturation. Chest pain may appear in patients with coronary disease.
pathologies.diagnosis: Sinus criteria with a rate above 100. Search for the cause: fever, pain, anxiety, hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, hyperthyroidism, stimulants or drugs, heart failure, MI. Differentiate from SVT: sinus tachycardia has visible P waves, gradual onset and a rate usually below 150.
pathologies.treatment: Identify and treat the underlying cause (antipyretics, analgesia, fluids or blood, oxygen, anxiety control). Do NOT cardiovert and do NOT give adenosine or antiarrhythmics. Beta blockers are used only for specific indications (for example hyperthyroidism) after the cause is addressed.
pathologies.recommendations: Reassess vital signs after treating the cause. Persistent sinus tachycardia in acute MI is a warning sign of heart failure or hypovolemia. Advise avoiding caffeine and stimulants.
key_learning_points: Sinus tachycardia is a symptom, not a disease: hunt for the cause.
Normal P waves, narrow QRS, gradual onset, rate usually below 150 bpm.
Never cardiovert sinus tachycardia.
sources: 1. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.
2. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Sinus tachycardia. litfl.com/ecg-library

required.explanation: Rate fits the teaching range for sinus tachycardia.
Sinus P waves remain present.
Each P conducts to a QRS.

supporting.explanation: Regular rhythm.
PR generally remains measurable.
QRS is narrow.
No ectopic premature pattern.

conflicts.explanation: Absent/flutter/fibrillatory atrial activity conflicts with sinus tachycardia.
Rates above the configured sinus-tachycardia teaching range should prompt another rhythm.
