pathologies.definition: A sinus rhythm in which the rate changes in cycles, most often with breathing: the heart speeds up when the person breathes in and slows down when they breathe out. It is a normal variant, especially in children and young adults.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 60-100 bpm, varying with respiration
Rhythm: Irregular in a cyclic (phasic) pattern
P wave: Normal and uniform, one before each QRS
PR interval: 0.12-0.20 s, constant
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Gradually shortens and lengthens; longest and shortest differ by more than 0.12 s
ST segment: Isoelectric
Other relevant characteristics: Disappears when the patient holds their breath. Every QRS still has a normal P wave, which separates it from atrial fibrillation.
simulation_parameters: R-R variability: Cyclic, about +/- 15-20%, repeating every 4-5 beats
Other: Respiratory cycle of roughly 4-5 seconds.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: None. The pulse feels irregular and changes with breathing. It is benign.
pathologies.diagnosis: Irregular rhythm with a normal, uniform P before every QRS and R-R intervals that change in cycles. Exclude atrial fibrillation (no P waves), PACs (isolated early beats) and sinus pauses. A breath-hold test makes the irregularity disappear.
pathologies.treatment: None required.
pathologies.recommendations: Reassure the patient. If it is not related to breathing and the patient is older or symptomatic, it may point to sinus node dysfunction and deserves further evaluation.
key_learning_points: Irregular, but every QRS still has a normal P wave.
The rate rises when breathing in and falls when breathing out.
Benign: no treatment, and do not confuse it with atrial fibrillation.
sources: 1. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Sinus arrhythmia. litfl.com/ecg-library
2. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 5: Sinus Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/5-sinus-rhythms

required.explanation: Sinus P waves are preserved.
Each P conducts to QRS.
R-R intervals vary in a cyclic pattern.

supporting.explanation: Typical teaching rate range.
PR remains constant.
QRS is narrow.
Cyclic respiratory variation supports sinus arrhythmia.

conflicts.explanation: Random irregularity conflicts with respiratory sinus arrhythmia.
Absent P waves conflict with sinus arrhythmia.

pathologies.module: MODULE 1 - SINUS RHYTHMS & SINUS NODE DISORDERS
pathologies.definition: The SA node fires on time, but the impulse is blocked before it leaves the node and reaches the atria. One P-QRS-T is missing, so the pause is an exact multiple (2x, 3x) of the normal P-P interval.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Baseline usually 40-100 bpm; average rate is lower because of the pauses
Rhythm: Regular with sudden pauses (regularly irregular)
P wave: Normal when present; absent during the pause
PR interval: Constant
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Constant, except for the pause, which equals 2x (or 3x) the basic interval
ST segment: Isoelectric

Other relevant characteristics: After the pause the underlying rhythm resumes ON TIME. In type I (Wenckebach) SA block the P-P interval shortens before the pause; in type II the pause is a fixed multiple.
simulation_parameters: R-R variability: None, except the dropped beat (pause exactly 2x the basic interval, occasionally 3x)
P-wave behavior: Normal; missing together with its QRS and T during the pause
Other: One or two pauses per 6-second strip.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Often none. With long or frequent pauses: lightheadedness, dizziness, fatigue, palpitations (skipped beats), near-syncope or syncope.
pathologies.diagnosis: Look for a pause with no P, QRS or T and MEASURE it: if it equals a multiple of the basic P-P interval, it is exit block; if it does not, it is sinus arrest. Consider Holter or event monitoring. Review drugs (digoxin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers), ischemia, hyperkalemia and sick sinus syndrome.
pathologies.treatment: Asymptomatic: observe and treat the cause (stop offending drugs). Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV (repeat every 3-5 min, maximum 3 mg), then transcutaneous pacing, dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min. Permanent pacemaker for symptomatic sinus node dysfunction without a reversible cause.
pathologies.recommendations: Continuous telemetry, pacing pads ready if pauses are frequent. Teach the patient to report dizziness or fainting. Refer to cardiology if symptomatic.
key_learning_points: The pause is an exact multiple (2x, 3x) of the normal P-P interval.
The SA node fires on time; the impulse just does not get out.
Pause plus dizziness or syncope: treat like symptomatic bradycardia.
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Sinoatrial exit block. litfl.com/ecg-library

required.explanation: Pause is a fixed multiple of the baseline sinus interval.
Normal sinus P waves are present outside the pause.

supporting.explanation: Regular baseline rhythm interrupted by a pause.
PR remains constant in conducted beats.
Conducted beats are usually narrow.
No premature beat explains the pause.

conflicts.explanation: A non-multiple pause favors sinus arrest rather than exit block.
Pacing activity suggests a paced mechanism.

pathologies.module: MODULE 1 - SINUS RHYTHMS & SINUS NODE DISORDERS
pathologies.definition: The SA node temporarily fails to generate an impulse, so there is no P wave and no QRS for a period of time. The pause is NOT a multiple of the normal P-P interval and is often ended by an escape beat from the AV junction or ventricles.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Baseline usually 40-100 bpm; lower overall because of the pause
Rhythm: Irregular because of the pause
P wave: Normal when present; absent during the pause
PR interval: Constant when P waves are present
QRS complex: Narrow (junctional escape beat) or wide (ventricular escape beat)
R-R interval: A pause of variable length that is not a multiple of the basic interval
ST segment: Isoelectric
Other relevant characteristics: Pauses of about 3 seconds or more are usually called arrest. The sinus rhythm may resume at a different timing than expected.
simulation_parameters: R-R variability: One long pause of 2.5-4 s (about 2.7-3.3x the basic interval, never an exact multiple)
P-wave behavior: Normal, then completely absent during the pause
Other: A junctional escape beat (no P, narrow QRS) ends the pause, then sinus rhythm resumes.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Dizziness, near-syncope or syncope, fatigue, confusion, palpitations. It can be asymptomatic during sleep. If no escape rhythm appears, the patient can progress to asystole.
pathologies.diagnosis: A pause with no P and no QRS whose length is not a multiple of the P-P interval. Look for the escape beat. Causes: increased vagal tone, sick sinus syndrome, inferior MI, digoxin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, amiodarone, hypoxia, hyperkalemia. Use Holter or event monitor; pauses above 3 s while awake are significant.
pathologies.treatment: Brief asymptomatic pauses: observe and treat the cause. Symptomatic: atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 min (maximum 3 mg), transcutaneous pacing, dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min. Permanent pacemaker for symptomatic sinus node dysfunction. If the pause becomes cardiac arrest with no pulse, start CPR.
pathologies.recommendations: Telemetry with pacing pads ready. Stop offending drugs and correct electrolytes. Explain the risk of syncope and refer to cardiology or electrophysiology.
key_learning_points: A pause with no P and no QRS; its length is NOT a multiple of the normal P-P interval.
Look for an escape beat (junctional or ventricular) that ends the pause.
Long pause plus symptoms: atropine, pacing, and think permanent pacemaker.
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 10: Other EKG Abnormalities (sinus pause, escape beats). LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/10-other-ekg-abnormalities

required.explanation: Pause is not an exact multiple of the baseline sinus interval.
Normal sinus P waves are present when sinus activity resumes.

supporting.explanation: A pause makes the rhythm irregular.
PR is constant when sinus P waves conduct.
QRS may remain narrow or reflect an escape beat.
No premature beat explains the pause.

conflicts.explanation: A fixed multiple pause favors sinus exit block.
Random continuous irregularity suggests another rhythm.

pathologies.definition: A normal sinus rhythm interrupted by an early beat from an irritable spot in the atria (premature atrial complex). The early beat comes before the next expected sinus beat and usually has a different-looking P wave.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Depends on the underlying sinus rhythm (usually 60-100 bpm)
Rhythm: Regular except for the premature beat(s)
P wave: Premature P' with a different shape (notched, biphasic, flattened or inverted); may be hidden in the previous T wave or not followed by a QRS (non-conducted PAC)
PR interval: May differ from the normal beats
QRS complex: Narrow (occasionally wide if conducted with aberrancy; absent if non-conducted)
R-R interval: The premature interval is shorter; the pause after is usually less than compensatory
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: Can occur in patterns: bigeminy (every 2nd beat), trigeminy (every 3rd), quadrigeminy (every 4th). A non-conducted PAC looks like a pause.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Base rhythm 60-90 bpm
R-R variability: 1-2 PACs per 10 beats, arriving at about 55-70% of the normal R-R; pause after about 105-115%
P-wave behavior: Premature P' with smaller or notched shape, PR 0.12-0.14 s
QRS duration: 0.08-0.10 s (same as sinus beats)
Other: The P' can deform the T wave of the preceding beat.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Often none. Palpitations, a "skipped beat" or fluttering in the chest. Triggers: caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stress, stimulants, hyperthyroidism, low potassium.
pathologies.diagnosis: Identify the underlying rhythm first, then find the early beat with an abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS. Differentiate: PJC has an absent or inverted P with short PR; PVC has a wide QRS, no P wave and a full compensatory pause.
pathologies.treatment: Usually none. Remove triggers, correct electrolytes and hypoxia. Beta blocker or calcium channel blocker only for bothersome symptoms. Frequent PACs should prompt evaluation for structural heart disease and atrial fibrillation risk.
pathologies.recommendations: Reduce caffeine, alcohol, nicotine and stress. Check electrolytes and thyroid function. Use an ambulatory monitor if PACs are frequent. Reassure the patient.
key_learning_points: An early beat with a different-looking P wave and a narrow QRS.
The pause after it is usually short (non-compensatory).
Benign, but frequent PACs can be a warning sign for atrial fibrillation.
sources: 1. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 6: Atrial Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/6-atrial-rhythms
2. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Premature atrial complex. litfl.com/ecg-library

required.explanation: A premature atrial complex is present.
The early beat is atrial in origin.

supporting.explanation: Premature P wave has an abnormal morphology.
PAC is usually followed by a narrow QRS.
Underlying rhythm is regular except for the premature beat.
Underlying sinus rate is commonly 60-100 bpm.

conflicts.explanation: Wide ventricular premature morphology favors PVC.
Pacing activity suggests a paced rhythm.

pathologies.definition: A very fast, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia that starts above the ventricles, usually from a reentry circuit in or near the AV node (AVNRT) or through an accessory pathway (AVRT). It typically starts and stops abruptly (paroxysmal SVT).
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 150-250 bpm (typically 160-220)
Rhythm: Very regular
P wave: Absent or hidden in the QRS/T; a retrograde P' may appear right after the QRS
PR interval: Not measurable
QRS complex: Narrow (< 0.12 s) unless there is aberrant conduction
R-R interval: Constant, almost perfectly regular
ST segment: Rate-related ST depression may be present
Other relevant characteristics: Abrupt onset and abrupt end. The rate does not change with breathing or activity. It can stop with vagal maneuvers or adenosine.
simulation_parameters: P-wave behavior: Not visible (hidden in the QRS/T)
Other: Small T wave and slight ST depression; optional abrupt start and stop.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Sudden pounding palpitations, dizziness, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, anxiety, sweating, frequent urination. Unstable patients have hypotension, altered mental status, syncope, shock or acute heart failure.
pathologies.diagnosis: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm or more with no visible sinus P waves and an abrupt onset. A 12-lead ECG helps exclude atrial flutter with 2:1 block (look for F waves) and sinus tachycardia. Check the baseline ECG for pre-excitation (delta wave).
pathologies.treatment: Unstable: synchronized cardioversion 50-100 J (sedate if awake). Stable: vagal maneuvers (modified Valsalva); adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push followed by 20 mL saline flush; if no conversion, 12 mg (may repeat 12 mg once). If it persists: diltiazem 15-20 mg (0.25 mg/kg) IV over 2 min or metoprolol 2.5-5 mg IV, and consult an expert. Catheter ablation is curative for recurrent SVT.
pathologies.recommendations: Record the ECG continuously during adenosine. Warn the patient about a brief feeling of chest tightness or flushing. Use a large proximal vein with a rapid flush. Reduce the adenosine dose (3 mg) with a central line, heart transplant, dipyridamole or carbamazepine. Teach vagal maneuvers and refer for ablation if recurrent.
key_learning_points: Regular, narrow, very fast (150-250 bpm) with no visible P waves and an abrupt onset.
Stable: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine 6 mg and 12 mg. Unstable: synchronized cardioversion.
Give adenosine as a fast push followed by a rapid saline flush.
sources: 1. Page RL, et al. 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia. Circulation. 2016;133(14):e506-e574.
2. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.

required.explanation: Rate fits the teaching range for SVT.
SVT is typically very regular.
Typical SVT is a narrow-complex tachycardia.

supporting.explanation: P waves may be hidden or retrograde.
PR is often not measurable at fast rates.
No isolated premature ectopic beat pattern.
No pacing spike pattern.

conflicts.explanation: Flutter waves favor atrial flutter.
Irregularly irregular rhythm favors AF rather than SVT.
A wide-complex tachycardia is not safely classifiable as generic SVT from these fields alone.

classifier.ambiguity_note: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia can have multiple supraventricular mechanisms; ECGenius classifies only the teaching label represented in the dataset.

pathologies.definition: Chaotic, disorganized electrical activity in the atria (350-600 impulses per minute) with no effective atrial contraction. The AV node lets impulses through at random, so the ventricles beat in a completely irregular way.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Atrial 350-600; ventricular variable, usually 60-170 bpm (rapid ventricular response above 100-110)
Rhythm: Irregularly irregular
P wave: Absent; fine or coarse fibrillatory (f) waves on the baseline
PR interval: Not measurable
QRS complex: Narrow (unless bundle branch block or aberrancy)
R-R interval: Completely random, no repeating pattern
ST segment: Non-specific, often rate-related depression

Other relevant characteristics: Loss of the atrial contribution to filling; blood stasis in the left atrial appendage raises stroke risk. Pulse deficit (apical rate higher than radial). Types: paroxysmal, persistent, permanent.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Ventricular 60-160 bpm (default about 90; rapid response 110-160)
R-R variability: Random, 40-150% of the mean, never repeating
P-wave behavior: Absent; irregular fibrillatory baseline 0.05-0.10 mV at about 4-9 Hz
Other: T waves change with the preceding R-R interval.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath, dizziness, chest discomfort, reduced exercise tolerance, syncope. Irregular pulse with pulse deficit. Unstable: hypotension, heart failure, ischemia, altered mental status. Stroke or TIA can be the first sign. Some patients have no symptoms.
pathologies.diagnosis: ECG (12-lead or rhythm strip of 30 s or more) with an irregularly irregular R-R interval and no distinct P waves. Use Holter, event monitors or wearables for paroxysmal AF. Work-up: thyroid function, electrolytes, echocardiogram, search for the cause. Calculate stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) and bleeding risk.
pathologies.treatment: Unstable (hypotension, ischemia, acute heart failure, altered mental status): synchronized cardioversion 120-200 J biphasic (sedate if awake). Stable: rate control with diltiazem 15-20 mg IV over 2 min (then 5-15 mg/h) or metoprolol 2.5-5 mg IV (use caution in decompensated heart failure); amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min or digoxin if heart failure or low blood pressure. Anticoagulation according to CHA2DS2-VASc (DOACs preferred over warfarin in most patients). Before elective cardioversion, AF lasting more than 48 h or of unknown duration needs anticoagulation for 3 weeks or a TEE. Rhythm control options: cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation. Avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF (WPW).
pathologies.recommendations: Educate about anticoagulation and stroke signs (FAST). Address alcohol, obesity, sleep apnea and blood pressure. Monitor heart rate, INR if on warfarin, and arrange regular follow-up.
key_learning_points: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals, no P waves and a quivering baseline.
Main dangers: stroke (anticoagulate by CHA2DS2-VASc) and a rapid ventricular rate.
Unstable: synchronized cardioversion 120-200 J. Stable: rate control.
sources: 1. Joglar JA, et al. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation. 2024;149(1):e1-e156.
2. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.

required.explanation: Irregularly irregular ventricular response is a hallmark feature.
No discrete consistent P waves are seen.

supporting.explanation: PR interval is not measurable.
QRS is usually narrow unless conduction disease/aberrancy is present.
No consistent P:QRS relationship.
No pacing spikes.

conflicts.explanation: Consistent sinus P waves conflict with AF.
A perfectly regular ventricular rhythm strongly conflicts with the teaching pattern for AF.

pathologies.definition: A rapid, organized reentrant circuit in the atria (usually the right atrium, around the cavotricuspid isthmus) firing at about 250-350 per minute. It creates "sawtooth" flutter waves, and the AV node conducts only some of them (for example 2:1 or 4:1).
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Atrial 250-350 bpm; ventricular usually 75-150 bpm
Rhythm: Atrial regular; ventricular regular if the ratio is fixed, irregular if it varies
P wave: No true P waves; flutter (F) waves with a sawtooth pattern, best seen in II, III, aVF and V1
PR interval: Not measurable
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Regular (fixed block) or regularly irregular (variable block)
ST segment: Hidden by the F waves
Other relevant characteristics: A ventricular rate fixed near 150 bpm suggests flutter with 2:1 block. Vagal maneuvers or adenosine slow the ventricular rate and reveal the F waves.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Atrial about 300 bpm (cycle 0.2 s); ventricular 150 (2:1) or 75 (4:1)
R-R variability: None when the ratio is fixed
P-wave behavior: Sawtooth F waves, about 0.10-0.15 mV
Other: T waves are buried in the flutter waves.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Palpitations, shortness of breath, fatigue, lightheadedness, chest discomfort. Rapid conduction can cause hypotension or syncope. There is a risk of blood clots and stroke, as in atrial fibrillation.
pathologies.diagnosis: Look for sawtooth F waves at about 300 per minute. Any regular narrow tachycardia at exactly about 150 bpm should make you think of flutter 2:1. Use vagal maneuvers or adenosine to unmask F waves. Rule out SVT and sinus tachycardia. Search for causes: heart disease, COPD, pulmonary embolism, hyperthyroidism, cardiac surgery, alcohol.
pathologies.treatment: Unstable: synchronized cardioversion 50-100 J (sedate if awake). Stable: rate control with diltiazem 15-20 mg IV over 2 min or a beta blocker; anticoagulation as in AF (CHA2DS2-VASc); rhythm control with cardioversion (very effective at low energy) or ibutilide. Catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus is first-line and highly successful for typical flutter.
pathologies.recommendations: Anticoagulate before and after cardioversion according to risk. Treat triggers (COPD, thyroid, pulmonary embolism). Refer for ablation. Educate about stroke symptoms.
key_learning_points: Sawtooth flutter waves at about 300 per minute instead of P waves.
A fixed ventricular rate near 150 bpm is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise.
Same stroke risk as AFib; ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus can cure typical flutter.
sources: 1. Page RL, et al. 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia. Circulation. 2016;133(14):e506-e574.
2. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.

required.explanation: Sawtooth/flutter atrial activity is the key feature.

supporting.explanation: PR is not measurable through flutter waves.
QRS is usually narrow.
A fixed 2:1 or variable AV conduction ratio supports flutter.
Ventricular rhythm can be regular with fixed block or irregular with variable block.

conflicts.explanation: Completely random irregularity without flutter waves favors AF.
Normal sinus P waves conflict with flutter.

classifier.ambiguity_note: A ventricular rate near 150 bpm is supportive of 2:1 flutter but is not mandatory.

pathologies.definition: The pacemaker site shifts from beat to beat between the SA node, the atria and the AV junction, producing at least three different P-wave shapes. With a rate below 100 bpm it is called wandering atrial pacemaker; at 100 bpm or more it becomes multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT).
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 40-100 bpm (usually 60-90)
Rhythm: Slightly irregular
P wave: At least 3 different morphologies (upright, flattened, notched, inverted); one P before each QRS
PR interval: Varies from beat to beat (shorter when the focus is near the AV junction)
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Varies slightly
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: The change in P shape is gradual. Common in COPD, healthy young people, athletes and older adults with vagal tone.
simulation_parameters: P-wave behavior: Cycles through at least 3 shapes (large upright, small, flat, inverted) with PR 0.10-0.16 s
Other: Increase the rate above 100 to make it MAT.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Usually none. Occasionally palpitations. Symptoms of the underlying disease (COPD shortness of breath, digoxin toxicity).
pathologies.diagnosis: A rhythm strip in one lead showing at least 3 different P-wave shapes with a rate below 100 bpm. Distinguish from atrial fibrillation (which has NO P waves), from isolated PACs, and from MAT (rate 100 or more).
pathologies.treatment: None for the rhythm itself: treat the underlying cause (COPD, hypoxia, digoxin toxicity, electrolyte disorders). For MAT: treat the lung disease, correct hypoxia, potassium and magnesium; magnesium 1-2 g IV; rate control with a calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) if needed. Cardioversion is ineffective.
pathologies.recommendations: Optimize respiratory status. Review medications (theophylline, beta agonists, digoxin). Reassure the patient; monitor for progression to MAT.
key_learning_points: At least three different P-wave shapes with a changing PR interval.
Below 100 bpm = wandering pacemaker; 100 bpm or more = multifocal atrial tachycardia (often COPD).
Benign by itself: treat the cause, not the rhythm.
sources: 1. Page RL, et al. 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia. Circulation. 2016;133(14):e506-e574.
2. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Wandering atrial pacemaker. litfl.com/ecg-library

required.explanation: At least three different P-wave morphologies are present.
Each atrial impulse is conducted to QRS in the teaching pattern.

supporting.explanation: Rate is generally 40-100 bpm.
Rhythm is mildly irregular.
PR varies as the atrial focus shifts.
QRS is narrow.

conflicts.explanation: Uniform sinus P waves conflict with wandering pacemaker.
A rate above 100 bpm suggests a different multifocal atrial rhythm rather than WAP.

pathologies.definition: A sinus rhythm in which conduction through the AV node is slow but complete: the PR interval is longer than 0.20 s, and every P wave is still followed by a QRS. It is a delay, not a true block.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Depends on the underlying rhythm (usually 60-100 bpm)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Normal, one before every QRS
PR interval: Longer than 0.20 s (more than one large box) and constant
QRS complex: Narrow (unless a bundle branch block is present)
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: At faster rates the P wave can sit close to the previous T wave. No beats are dropped.
simulation_parameters: P-wave behavior: Present, upright, all conducted
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Usually none. Rarely fatigue or dizziness when the PR is very long (loss of AV synchrony, "pacemaker-like" syndrome).
pathologies.diagnosis: PR longer than 0.20 s and constant, with every P followed by a QRS. Search for causes: high vagal tone, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone, inferior MI, myocarditis, endocarditis (aortic root abscess), hyperkalemia, Lyme disease, degenerative disease.
pathologies.treatment: None if asymptomatic. Review and adjust AV-nodal drugs. Monitor for progression to higher-degree blocks. Pacing is considered only with a very long PR (above 0.30 s) and symptoms.
pathologies.recommendations: Repeat ECGs over time. Be careful when adding AV-nodal blocking drugs. Watch closely in acute MI, endocarditis and Lyme carditis.
key_learning_points: Every P conducts, but the PR interval is longer than 0.20 s and constant.
Usually benign: review AV-nodal drugs and watch for progression.
First-degree means a long PR with nothing dropped.
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 9: Atrioventricular Blocks. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/9-atrioventricular-blocks

required.explanation: PR is prolonged and constant.
Every P still conducts to QRS.

supporting.explanation: Sinus P waves are present.
Rhythm is regular.
QRS is often narrow.
Underlying sinus rate is commonly 60-100 bpm.

conflicts.explanation: Dropped beats indicate second-degree block, not first-degree.
A normal PR conflicts with first-degree AV block.

pathologies.definition: Second-degree AV block Mobitz I (Wenckebach). The PR interval gets longer with each beat until one P wave is not conducted and a QRS is dropped. The block is within the AV node.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Atrial normal; ventricular slightly lower because of dropped beats (often 50-80 bpm)
Rhythm: Regularly irregular (grouped beating); P-P interval is regular
P wave: Normal; one P per group is not followed by a QRS
PR interval: Progressively lengthens until a beat is dropped, then resets
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Progressively shortens before the pause; the pause is less than 2x the shortest R-R
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: Group ratios such as 3:2, 4:3, 5:4. The first PR after the pause is the shortest.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Atrial 63-75 bpm (P-P 0.8-0.95 s)
P-wave behavior: Regular P waves; one non-conducted P per group
Other: 4:3 pattern with PR 0.16, 0.27, 0.38 s, then a dropped beat.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Often none, especially during sleep or in athletes. Occasionally dizziness, lightheadedness, fatigue, skipped beats. Syncope is rare.
pathologies.diagnosis: Grouped beating with progressive PR lengthening, a dropped QRS and resetting after the pause. Usually benign because the block is in the AV node. Causes: high vagal tone, inferior MI, digoxin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, myocarditis.
pathologies.treatment: Asymptomatic: observe. Symptomatic or unstable bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV (often effective because the block is in the AV node), then transcutaneous pacing if it fails. Treat the cause and stop offending drugs.
pathologies.recommendations: Monitor, especially in inferior MI. Risk of progression is low. A permanent pacemaker is rarely needed unless symptomatic or the block is infranodal. Teach the patient to report fainting.
key_learning_points: "Longer, longer, longer, drop!": the PR lengthens until a QRS is dropped.
The block is in the AV node: usually benign, and atropine often works.
Group beating, with R-R intervals shortening before each pause.
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 9: Atrioventricular Blocks. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/9-atrioventricular-blocks

required.explanation: PR progressively lengthens until a QRS is dropped.
At least one P wave is not conducted.

supporting.explanation: Grouped beating produces regular irregularity.
Sinus P waves continue through the sequence.
QRS is commonly narrow in nodal Wenckebach.

conflicts.explanation: Constant PR with sudden dropped beats favors Mobitz II.
2:1 conduction cannot be reliably labeled Mobitz I from the ratio alone.

pathologies.definition: Second-degree AV block Mobitz II. Some P waves suddenly fail to conduct WITHOUT any earlier PR lengthening. The block is usually below the AV node (His-Purkinje system), so it is unpredictable and can progress to complete heart block.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Atrial normal (60-100); ventricular lower depending on how many P waves are blocked
Rhythm: P-P regular; R-R regular with sudden pauses
P wave: Normal; some are not followed by a QRS
PR interval: Constant in every conducted beat (normal or prolonged)
QRS complex: Often wide (bundle branch block); can be narrow
R-R interval: Pause equals 2x the basic interval when a single beat is dropped
ST segment: Normal, or changes related to bundle branch block
Other relevant characteristics: High-grade block if 2 or more consecutive P waves are blocked. Can progress suddenly to third-degree block.
simulation_parameters: R-R variability: Random dropped beats (about 1 in every 3-5 P waves)
P-wave behavior: Regular P waves, PR constant at 0.18-0.22 s
Other: No lengthening of PR before the dropped beat.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Dizziness, presyncope or syncope, fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, hypotension, slow pulse. Stokes-Adams attacks and risk of asystole.
pathologies.diagnosis: Constant PR interval with a sudden non-conducted P wave, usually with a wide QRS. Common in anterior MI and conduction system disease. Needs cardiology evaluation. Differentiate from Type I: here the PR does NOT change.
pathologies.treatment: Place transcutaneous pacing pads early; pacing is the key treatment when symptomatic or unstable. Atropine may be ineffective or even worsen an infranodal block. Bridge with dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min, then transvenous pacing. A permanent pacemaker is usually indicated.
pathologies.recommendations: Admit to a monitored bed with pads on. Avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs. Treat MI or other causes. Arrange cardiology for a permanent pacemaker.
key_learning_points: The PR interval is constant, then a QRS suddenly drops without warning.
Infranodal block, often with a wide QRS; it can progress to complete heart block.
Pads on early: pacing is the treatment, and atropine may not work (or may make it worse).
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.

required.explanation: Conducted beats keep a constant PR before sudden dropped QRS complexes.
Some P waves fail to conduct.

supporting.explanation: Sudden dropped beats interrupt an otherwise regular rhythm.
Atrial rhythm continues regularly.
QRS may be wide or narrow; width is supportive but not defining.
A dropped beat can create a pause equal to a multiple of the baseline cycle.

conflicts.explanation: Progressive PR lengthening favors Mobitz I.
2:1 AV block should remain its own classification when every other P is blocked.

pathologies.definition: A second-degree AV block in which every second P wave fails to conduct (2 P waves for each QRS). Because the PR interval never changes, it is impossible to classify it as Type I or Type II from this pattern alone.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Ventricular rate is half of the atrial rate (for example atrial 100-120, ventricular 50-60)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Normal; two P waves for every QRS, one conducted and one blocked (the blocked P can hide in the T wave)
PR interval: Constant in the conducted beats (normal or prolonged)
QRS complex: Narrow suggests a nodal block (Type I-like); wide suggests an infranodal block (Type II-like)
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: The hidden P waves can make it look like sinus bradycardia. Look for a notched or distorted T wave.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Atrial 110-120 bpm (P-P 0.50-0.56 s); ventricular about 55-60 bpm
P-wave behavior: Regular P waves, every second one blocked
Other: PR fixed at about 0.16 s.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: May be asymptomatic. When the ventricular rate is slow: dizziness, fatigue, presyncope or syncope, hypotension.
pathologies.diagnosis: Two P waves per QRS with a fixed PR interval. Check the T waves for hidden P waves. Longer strips or maneuvers may reveal 3:2 conduction (Type I) or randomly dropped beats (Type II). Narrow QRS points to Type I; wide QRS points to Type II. Treat as high risk until clarified.
pathologies.treatment: Manage according to the site of the block. Symptomatic with narrow QRS (likely nodal): atropine 1 mg IV, then pacing if it fails. Wide QRS or infranodal block: pacing pads on, transcutaneous pacing, dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min, and cardiology for a permanent pacemaker. Stable with narrow QRS: observe and monitor.
pathologies.recommendations: Continuous monitoring. When in doubt, treat as Mobitz II. Review AV-nodal drugs. An electrophysiology study may be needed.
key_learning_points: Two P waves for every QRS (2:1); the second P is blocked.
You cannot tell Type I from Type II with 2:1 alone: the QRS width is the clue.
Wide QRS or symptoms: treat like Mobitz II (pacing).
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Second-degree AV block (2:1). litfl.com/ecg-library

required.explanation: Two P waves are present for each QRS.
AV conduction ratio is 2:1.

supporting.explanation: The ventricular rhythm is typically regular.
Regular sinus P waves are present.
Conducted beats have a constant measurable PR.
QRS width may suggest level of block but does not by itself define Mobitz type.

conflicts.explanation: 1:1 conduction conflicts with 2:1 AV block.
Complete AV dissociation indicates third-degree block.

classifier.ambiguity_note: Do not force 2:1 AV block into Mobitz I or II based on the surface rhythm fields alone.

pathologies.definition: Complete failure of conduction between the atria and the ventricles. The atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation), and the ventricles are driven by a slow junctional or ventricular escape rhythm.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Atrial 60-100 bpm; ventricular 20-60 bpm (junctional escape 40-60, ventricular escape 20-40)
Rhythm: P-P regular and R-R regular, but independent of each other
P wave: Normal, with NO relationship to the QRS; they march through the QRS and T waves
PR interval: Variable (no true PR)
QRS complex: Narrow (junctional escape) or wide (ventricular escape)
R-R interval: Regular and slow
ST segment: Depends on the QRS
Other relevant characteristics: Cannon A waves in the neck. The escape rate and QRS width predict stability: slower and wider is more dangerous.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Atrial 68-84 bpm; ventricular escape 30-48 bpm
P-wave behavior: Regular P waves marching independently through the QRS
QRS duration: 0.08-0.10 s (junctional variant) or 0.12-0.16 s (ventricular variant)
Other: Variant chosen at random or fixed for teaching.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Fatigue, dizziness, syncope (Stokes-Adams), chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, hypotension, very slow pulse, heart failure, cannon A waves, and sudden cardiac arrest.
pathologies.diagnosis: AV dissociation with an atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate and a regular, slow escape rhythm. Look for causes: inferior or anterior MI, fibrosis of the conduction system, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, hyperkalemia, myocarditis, Lyme disease, cardiac surgery or TAVR, endocarditis.
pathologies.treatment: Symptomatic or unstable: immediate transcutaneous pacing. Give atropine 1 mg IV while preparing (may not work if the block is infranodal). Dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min as a bridge, then transvenous pacing. Permanent pacemaker is definitive unless the cause is reversible. Treat reversible causes (stop drugs, correct potassium, antibiotics for Lyme carditis). Stable: monitored bed, pads on, cardiology.
pathologies.recommendations: Do not delay pacing while waiting for atropine to work. Avoid drugs that slow conduction. Keep pads on standby and watch for asystole. Explain the pacemaker to the patient.
key_learning_points: P waves and QRS complexes are completely independent (AV dissociation).
Regular but slow ventricular rate (20-60 bpm) from an escape pacemaker.
Unstable: transcutaneous pacing now; atropine is a bridge, not the cure.
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.

required.explanation: Atrial and ventricular activity are independent.
There is complete AV dissociation.

supporting.explanation: The escape rhythm is usually regular.
There is no fixed PR relationship.
Escape QRS may be narrow or wide depending on origin.
Typical ventricular escape rate in the dataset is 20-60 bpm.

conflicts.explanation: 1:1 AV conduction conflicts with complete heart block.
A constant PR with 1:1 conduction fits first-degree, not third-degree block.

pathologies.definition: A normal sinus rhythm interrupted by an early beat that starts in the AV junction (premature junctional complex). The impulse reaches the ventricles normally, so the QRS is narrow, but the P wave is absent, inverted or abnormally timed.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Depends on the underlying sinus rhythm
Rhythm: Regular except for the premature beat(s)
P wave: Absent, inverted before the QRS, or inverted right after the QRS in the premature beat
PR interval: Shorter than 0.12 s when a P wave precedes the QRS
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: The premature beat is early; a pause usually follows
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: Often linked to digoxin toxicity. The early beat looks like a PAC, but without a normal P.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Base rhythm 60-90 bpm
R-R variability: 1 PJC per 10 beats at about 64% of the base R-R, then a pause of about 110%
P-wave behavior: Inverted P (amplitude about -0.09 mV) with PR about 0.08 s, or absent
QRS duration: 0.08-0.10 s (same as sinus beats)
Other: Optional retrograde P after the QRS.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Usually none. Occasionally palpitations or a skipped beat. Ask about digoxin, caffeine and stimulants; consider ischemia and electrolyte problems.
pathologies.diagnosis: A premature beat with a narrow QRS and NO normal P wave: inverted P with short PR, absent P, or retrograde P after the QRS. Differentiate from PAC (different but usually upright P with PR of 0.12 s or more) and PVC (wide QRS).
pathologies.treatment: Usually none. Treat the cause: hold digoxin if toxicity is suspected, check digoxin level, potassium and magnesium, treat ischemia, reduce caffeine and stimulants. Beta blocker only if frequent and symptomatic.
pathologies.recommendations: Check digoxin level and electrolytes. Monitor for runs of junctional rhythm or tachycardia. Reassure the patient.
key_learning_points: An early narrow-QRS beat with an inverted, absent or very short-PR P wave.
Think digoxin toxicity, ischemia or stimulants.
Usually benign: treat the cause, not the beat.
sources: 1. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Premature junctional complex. litfl.com/ecg-library
2. Aehlert B. ECGs Made Easy. Elsevier.

required.explanation: A premature junctional complex is present.
The premature beat originates from the junction.

supporting.explanation: The premature beat may have an inverted/retrograde or absent P wave.
PR is short when a retrograde P precedes QRS.
PJC is usually narrow.
Underlying sinus rhythm is interrupted by an early beat.

conflicts.explanation: Abnormal premature P before QRS favors PAC.
Wide premature ventricular morphology favors PVC.

pathologies.definition: An escape rhythm that starts in the AV junction (AV node and bundle of His). It takes over when the SA node fails or is too slow, firing at its natural rate of 40-60 bpm.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 40-60 bpm (below 40 is called junctional bradycardia)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Inverted in II, III, aVF; or absent; or after the QRS
PR interval: Shorter than 0.12 s if a P wave precedes the QRS
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: Loss of atrial contribution can lower cardiac output. Often follows a sinus pause or slowing.
simulation_parameters: P-wave behavior: Inverted with PR about 0.08 s, absent, or retrograde after the QRS
Other: T wave upright, isoelectric baseline.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Often none. If the rate is low or AV synchrony is lost: fatigue, dizziness, hypotension, syncope, cannon A waves. Signs of digoxin toxicity: nausea, visual changes, confusion.
pathologies.diagnosis: A regular, slow, narrow-complex rhythm with abnormal P waves. Causes: SA node dysfunction, high vagal tone, inferior MI, digoxin toxicity, beta blockers or calcium channel blockers, cardiac surgery.
pathologies.treatment: Asymptomatic: observe and treat the cause (stop digoxin, oxygen). Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 min (maximum 3 mg), transcutaneous pacing, dopamine or epinephrine infusion. Avoid digoxin. Do not suppress the escape rhythm with antiarrhythmics.
pathologies.recommendations: Check digoxin level and electrolytes. Monitor. Avoid adding AV-nodal blocking drugs. Remember that the junctional escape is protecting the patient.
key_learning_points: Regular, slow (40-60 bpm), narrow QRS with inverted, absent or hidden P waves.
It is an escape rhythm: the backup when the SA node fails.
Suspect digoxin toxicity; treat only if symptomatic (atropine, pacing).
sources: 1. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 7: Junctional Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/7-junctional-rhythms
2. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.

required.explanation: Rate fits junctional escape rhythm.
P waves are absent, inverted, or retrograde.

supporting.explanation: Junctional rhythm is regular.
PR is short if retrograde P precedes QRS, or not measurable if P is hidden/after QRS.
QRS is usually narrow.
This is a sustained rhythm, not an isolated premature beat.

conflicts.explanation: Normal sinus P waves conflict with a junctional rhythm.
Rates above 60 move toward accelerated junctional rhythm in this curriculum.

pathologies.definition: A junctional rhythm faster than the junction's natural 40-60 bpm, but not above 100 bpm, caused by increased automaticity of the AV junction. It is called "accelerated" because the normal rate of the junction is slower than that of the SA node.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 61-100 bpm
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Inverted, absent, or after the QRS
PR interval: Shorter than 0.12 s if a P wave precedes the QRS
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Normal
Other relevant characteristics: The rate looks like normal sinus rhythm, but the P waves are abnormal or missing. The sinus node may continue at a slower rate (AV dissociation).
simulation_parameters: Other: Isoelectric baseline; upright T wave.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Usually none. Possible fatigue or palpitations. Digoxin toxicity signs: nausea, vomiting, visual changes (yellow halos), confusion.
pathologies.diagnosis: Regular narrow rhythm at 60-100 bpm with abnormal or absent P waves. Correlate with medications and ischemia. Check digoxin level, potassium, magnesium and troponin. Causes: digoxin toxicity, inferior MI, cardiac surgery, myocarditis.
pathologies.treatment: Usually none: it is often self-limited. Treat the cause: hold digoxin, correct electrolytes, oxygen. For severe digoxin toxicity: DigiFab (digoxin-specific antibody fragments). Avoid electrical cardioversion in digoxin toxicity unless the patient is unstable.
pathologies.recommendations: Monitor on telemetry. Measure digoxin level. Watch for progression to junctional tachycardia or ventricular arrhythmias in digoxin toxicity. Reduce stimulants.
key_learning_points: Junctional rhythm, but at 60-100 bpm: faster than the junction's natural 40-60.
Absent or inverted P waves with a narrow QRS.
Classic culprit: digoxin toxicity (also inferior MI and cardiac surgery).
sources: 1. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 7: Junctional Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/7-junctional-rhythms
2. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Accelerated junctional rhythm. litfl.com/ecg-library

required.explanation: Rate fits accelerated junctional rhythm.
P waves are absent, inverted, or retrograde.

supporting.explanation: Rhythm is regular.
PR is short if visible or not measurable.
QRS is typically narrow.
Sustained junctional rhythm rather than an isolated PJC.

conflicts.explanation: A slower rate fits junctional rhythm.
A faster rate fits junctional tachycardia in this curriculum.

pathologies.definition: A junctional rhythm above 100 bpm caused by increased automaticity in the AV junction (not a reentry circuit). It has a gradual warm-up, unlike the abrupt start of AVNRT.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 101-180 bpm (often 100-130)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Inverted, absent, or after the QRS
PR interval: Shorter than 0.12 s if a P wave precedes the QRS
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Normal or mild depression
Other relevant characteristics: Gradual onset and offset. It often does not stop with adenosine, vagal maneuvers or cardioversion.
simulation_parameters: Other: Isoelectric baseline; small T wave.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Palpitations, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, fatigue; hypotension if severe; loss of atrial kick. Signs of digoxin toxicity: nausea, visual changes, confusion.
pathologies.diagnosis: Regular narrow tachycardia with abnormal P waves and a gradual onset, not responding to adenosine or vagal maneuvers. Look for digoxin toxicity, ischemia, post-cardiac surgery, myocarditis, COPD. Check digoxin level, potassium and magnesium.
pathologies.treatment: Treat the cause first: stop digoxin, correct potassium and magnesium, oxygen, analgesia; DigiFab for severe digoxin toxicity. If needed and stable: beta blocker, calcium channel blocker (diltiazem 15-20 mg IV over 2 min) or amiodarone (150 mg IV over 10 min). Synchronized cardioversion only if unstable; it is often ineffective and can trigger ventricular fibrillation in digoxin toxicity. Avoid digoxin.
pathologies.recommendations: Close monitoring. Check digoxin level and electrolytes. Consult an expert. Do not keep repeating cardioversion if it does not work: the rhythm is automatic.
key_learning_points: Regular, narrow tachycardia above 100 bpm with absent or inverted P waves.
It is automatic (not reentrant), so it often ignores adenosine and cardioversion.
Hunt for digoxin toxicity, ischemia and post-cardiac-surgery causes.
sources: 1. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 7: Junctional Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/7-junctional-rhythms
2. Page RL, et al. 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia. Circulation. 2016;133(14):e506-e574.

required.explanation: Rate fits junctional tachycardia in the dataset.
P waves are absent, inverted, or retrograde.

supporting.explanation: Rhythm is regular.
PR is short if visible or not measurable.
QRS is typically narrow.
Sustained rhythm rather than isolated PJC.

conflicts.explanation: Normal sinus P waves favor sinus tachycardia.
Wide-complex tachycardia requires a different differential.

pathologies.definition: A normal sinus rhythm interrupted by an early beat that starts in the ventricles (premature ventricular complex). The impulse spreads slowly through the ventricles, so the QRS is wide and bizarre, and it is followed by a pause.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Depends on the underlying rhythm (usually 60-100 bpm)
Rhythm: Regular except for the premature beat(s)
P wave: None before the PVC (the sinus P may be hidden in the wide QRS or T)
PR interval: Not applicable to the PVC
QRS complex: Wide (more than 0.12 s), bizarre, with a T wave pointing the opposite way
R-R interval: The premature interval is short, followed by a full compensatory pause (the two intervals together equal 2x the normal R-R)
ST segment: Discordant (opposite to the QRS)
Other relevant characteristics: Patterns: bigeminy, trigeminy, couplets. Three or more in a row is ventricular tachycardia. Multifocal PVCs and R-on-T are higher risk.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Base rhythm 60-90 bpm
R-R variability: 1-2 PVCs per 11 beats at about 60% of the base R-R, followed by about 140% (compensatory pause)
P-wave behavior: Normal in sinus beats; absent in the PVC
QRS duration: 0.12-0.16 s in the PVC, taller than sinus beats, inverted T wave
Other: Optionally vary morphology for multifocal PVCs.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Often none. Palpitations, skipped or "heavy" beats, dizziness, weak pulse for the premature beat. Very frequent PVCs (burden above about 10-15%) can lead to cardiomyopathy and heart failure symptoms. Chest pain if ischemia is the cause.
pathologies.diagnosis: Identify the wide premature complex with no preceding P wave and a compensatory pause. Note the frequency and morphology. Correlate with ischemia, low potassium or magnesium, hypoxia, caffeine and structural heart disease (echocardiogram). Use Holter to measure burden.
pathologies.treatment: Isolated and asymptomatic: no treatment. Correct potassium, magnesium, hypoxia and ischemia; reduce caffeine and stimulants. Beta blocker or calcium channel blocker for symptoms; antiarrhythmics or ablation for very frequent PVCs or cardiomyopathy. In acute MI, do not give prophylactic antiarrhythmics. Runs of VT: follow the VT algorithm.
pathologies.recommendations: Watch for R-on-T, couplets, multifocal PVCs and runs of VT. Check potassium and magnesium. Continue monitoring and educate the patient.
key_learning_points: Early, wide, bizarre QRS with no preceding P wave and a full compensatory pause.
Isolated PVCs are often benign; three or more in a row is ventricular tachycardia.
Correct potassium, magnesium, hypoxia and ischemia; do not suppress PVCs in MI.
sources: 1. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 8: Ventricular Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/8-ventricular-rhythms
2. Al-Khatib SM, et al. 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for Management of Patients With Ventricular Arrhythmias and the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death. Circulation. 2018;138(13):e272-e391.

required.explanation: A premature ventricular complex is present.
The premature beat is ventricular in origin.

supporting.explanation: PVC has a wide/bizarre premature QRS.
No P precedes the PVC; sinus P waves may continue elsewhere.
Underlying rhythm is interrupted by the premature beat.
A compensatory pause supports PVC.

conflicts.explanation: A premature abnormal P with narrow QRS favors PAC.
A narrow premature beat with retrograde P favors PJC.

pathologies.definition: A ventricular escape rhythm at 20-40 bpm that takes over when the SA node, atria and AV junction all fail to pace the heart. The QRS is wide because the impulse starts in the ventricles. It is the heart's last backup.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 20-40 bpm
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Absent (or dissociated from the QRS)
PR interval: Not applicable
QRS complex: Wide (more than 0.12 s) and bizarre
R-R interval: Regular and long
ST segment: Discordant (opposite to the QRS)
Other relevant characteristics: A "dying heart" rhythm that can degenerate into asystole or pulseless electrical activity (PEA).
simulation_parameters: Other: Discordant T wave; long flat baseline between complexes.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Hypotension, syncope, altered mental status, shock, cold and pale skin, weak or absent pulse. The patient may be pulseless (PEA).
pathologies.diagnosis: Slow, regular, wide-complex rhythm without P waves. ALWAYS check for a pulse. Causes: complete heart block, failure of higher pacemakers, extensive MI, hyperkalemia, drug overdose (digoxin, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, tricyclics), hypoxia, acidosis, hypothermia.
pathologies.treatment: No pulse: this is PEA, start CPR (epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 min; treat the Hs and Ts). With a pulse and unstable: transcutaneous pacing; atropine 1 mg IV (unlikely to work); dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min; treat reversible causes (for example IV calcium for hyperkalemia). Do NOT give lidocaine or other antiarrhythmics to suppress it.
pathologies.recommendations: Pads on immediately. Search rapidly for reversible causes. Call an expert and arrange early transvenous pacing.
key_learning_points: Slow (20-40 bpm), regular, wide QRS, no P waves.
It is the heart's last backup: never suppress it with lidocaine or amiodarone.
Always check for a pulse: without one it is PEA, so start CPR.
sources: 1. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.
2. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 8: Ventricular Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/8-ventricular-rhythms

required.explanation: Rate fits the curriculum range for idioventricular rhythm.
Ventricular escape rhythm produces wide QRS complexes.

supporting.explanation: Rhythm is usually regular.
P waves are absent or dissociated.
No fixed PR relationship.
Sustained ventricular rhythm, not an isolated PVC.

conflicts.explanation: A faster ventricular rhythm moves toward AIVR in this curriculum.
A narrow QRS conflicts with idioventricular origin.

pathologies.definition: A regular ventricular rhythm at 41-100 bpm caused by increased automaticity of a ventricular focus. It is like a slow ventricular tachycardia, usually brief and well tolerated, and it is a classic sign of reperfusion after a heart attack.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: 41-100 bpm (often 60-100)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Absent, or dissociated (sinus P waves may march through)
PR interval: Not applicable
QRS complex: Wide (more than 0.12 s)
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Discordant

Other relevant characteristics: Often starts and stops gradually, with fusion beats, when the sinus rate slows or speeds up. Seen after reperfusion (thrombolysis or angioplasty), digoxin toxicity, cocaine and myocarditis.
simulation_parameters: Other: Discordant T wave; optional fusion beats at the start and end.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Usually none. Loss of AV synchrony can occasionally cause hypotension, palpitations or dizziness. Generally well tolerated.
pathologies.diagnosis: Regular wide-complex rhythm at 41-100 bpm. Compare with idioventricular rhythm (below 40) and VT (above 100). Context helps: recent reperfusion after MI. Check pulse and blood pressure.
pathologies.treatment: Usually none: it is self-limited. Observe on telemetry and treat the cause (for example digoxin toxicity). Avoid routine antiarrhythmics. If there is hemodynamic compromise: atropine to speed the sinus rate, or pacing; use antiarrhythmic therapy only if it degenerates into VT.
pathologies.recommendations: Continuous monitoring. Correct electrolytes. Watch for degeneration into ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation. Check perfusion regularly.
key_learning_points: Wide, regular ventricular rhythm at 41-100 bpm (a slow VT).
A classic reperfusion rhythm after a heart attack, usually harmless.
Do not treat by reflex: observe, and act only if perfusion suffers.
sources: 1. Al-Khatib SM, et al. 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for Management of Patients With Ventricular Arrhythmias and the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death. Circulation. 2018;138(13):e272-e391.
2. Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL) ECG Library: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm. litfl.com/ecg-library

required.explanation: Rate fits the dataset range for AIVR.
AIVR is a wide-complex ventricular rhythm.

supporting.explanation: Rhythm is typically regular.
P waves may be absent or dissociated.
No fixed PR interval.
Sustained rhythm, not an isolated PVC.

conflicts.explanation: A slower ventricular rhythm fits IVR.
A faster wide-complex ventricular rhythm raises concern for VT.

pathologies.definition: Three or more consecutive ventricular beats at more than 100 bpm. It is called sustained if it lasts more than 30 seconds or causes collapse. In monomorphic VT every QRS has the same shape. It can occur with a pulse or without a pulse (cardiac arrest).
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: More than 100 bpm (typically 150-250)
Rhythm: Regular (monomorphic)
P wave: Absent, or AV dissociation with P waves hidden in the QRS
PR interval: Not applicable
QRS complex: Wide (more than 0.12 s), uniform, bizarre
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Discordant
Other relevant characteristics: Fusion and capture beats and AV dissociation support VT. A wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise.
simulation_parameters: Other: Constant amplitude of about 1 mV, no isoelectric baseline.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, syncope, hypotension, shock, altered mental status. Pulseless VT is cardiac arrest.
pathologies.diagnosis: Regular wide-complex tachycardia above 100 bpm. Check the pulse FIRST. If stable, obtain a 12-lead ECG and consult an expert. Causes: MI, ischemic scar, cardiomyopathy, low potassium or magnesium, QT-prolonging drugs.
pathologies.treatment: No pulse: CPR plus defibrillation 200 J biphasic (unsynchronized), epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 min, amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg (or lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg); treat Hs and Ts. Pulse and unstable: synchronized cardioversion 100 J (sedate if awake; increase energy if needed). Pulse and stable: amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min (repeat as needed), or procainamide 20-50 mg/min up to 17 mg/kg, or sotalol; consult an expert. Adenosine only if regular and monomorphic and uncertain. Avoid verapamil and diltiazem in wide-complex tachycardia of unknown origin. Magnesium 1-2 g IV for torsades or long QT.
pathologies.recommendations: Pads on early. Correct potassium and magnesium. Avoid QT-prolonging drugs. Evaluate for coronary disease and for an implantable defibrillator (ICD) after the event.
key_learning_points: Regular, wide, fast (above 100 bpm) with no P waves: treat any wide tachycardia as VT.
Check the pulse first: no pulse means CPR and defibrillation; pulse and unstable means synchronized cardioversion.
Stable with pulse: amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min; avoid verapamil.
sources: 1. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.
2. Al-Khatib SM, et al. 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for Management of Patients With Ventricular Arrhythmias and the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death. Circulation. 2018;138(13):e272-e391.

required.explanation: Tachycardic ventricular rate.
VT is a wide-complex rhythm in this teaching set.

supporting.explanation: Monomorphic VT is generally regular.
P waves may be absent or dissociated.
No fixed PR relationship.
This is a sustained tachycardia rather than an isolated PVC.

conflicts.explanation: A narrow-complex tachycardia does not fit the teaching pattern for VT.
Pacing spikes preceding QRS favor a paced ventricular rhythm.

classifier.ambiguity_note: In real clinical practice, wide-complex tachycardia has a broader differential. ECGenius is an educational pattern matcher and should not claim clinical certainty.

pathologies.definition: Chaotic, disorganized electrical activity in the ventricles. The heart quivers instead of pumping, so there is no pulse and no blood flow. It is a cardiac arrest rhythm and is shockable.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Not measurable (chaotic)
Rhythm: Chaotic and irregular
P wave: None
PR interval: None
QRS complex: None identifiable (coarse or fine undulations)
R-R interval: None
ST segment: None identifiable
Other relevant characteristics: Coarse VF (larger waves) responds better to shock than fine VF. Fine VF can look like asystole: check leads and gain.
simulation_parameters: Heart rate range: Not applicable (chaotic activity at about 3.5-8 Hz)
Other: Chaotic waveform, amplitude 0.3-0.9 mV, waxing and waning; no organized QRS.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: Sudden collapse, unresponsive, no pulse, no normal breathing (or agonal gasps), cyanosis. Preceded sometimes by chest pain, palpitations or syncope.
pathologies.diagnosis: Unresponsive, pulseless patient with a chaotic rhythm. Confirm that electrodes are attached and it is not artifact, and check the pulse. Causes: MI or ischemia, degeneration of VT, electrolyte disorders, electrocution, drugs, hypothermia, cardiomyopathy, Brugada or long QT syndrome, commotio cordis.
pathologies.treatment: Start high-quality CPR immediately (100-120 compressions per min, depth 5-6 cm, full recoil, minimal interruptions) and defibrillate as soon as possible: 200 J biphasic (or manufacturer's dose), then resume CPR for 2 min. IV/IO access; epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 min; amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, then 150 mg (or lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5-0.75 mg/kg). Treat reversible causes (Hs and Ts). After return of circulation: 12-lead ECG, oxygenation and ventilation targets, blood pressure support, temperature control.
pathologies.recommendations: Use an AED early. Assign team roles and check the rhythm every 2 minutes. Arrange ICD evaluation after survival. Debrief the team and support the family.
key_learning_points: Chaotic wavy baseline: no P, no QRS, no pulse. It is cardiac arrest.
Shock as soon as possible: CPR plus defibrillation 200 J, then CPR for 2 minutes.
Epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 min; amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock; look for the Hs and Ts.
sources: 1. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.
2. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 8: Ventricular Rhythms. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/8-ventricular-rhythms

required.explanation: No organized measurable ventricular rate.
Electrical activity is chaotic.
No identifiable organized QRS complexes.

supporting.explanation: No organized P waves.
No organized P:QRS relationship.
PR interval is not applicable.
No pacing pattern explains the tracing.

conflicts.explanation: A regular organized rhythm conflicts with VF.
Identifiable repeating QRS complexes argue against VF.

pathologies.definition: A rhythm driven by an artificial pacemaker that stimulates the atrium. A tiny vertical pacing spike appears before each P wave, and the impulse then conducts normally through the AV node, giving a narrow QRS.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Set by the pacemaker (lower rate usually 60-80 bpm)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Pacing spike followed by a paced P wave (its shape differs from a sinus P)
PR interval: Normal (0.12-0.20 s) because conduction is through the native AV node
QRS complex: Narrow
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Normal

Other relevant characteristics: Capture means every spike is followed by a P wave. Sensing means the pacemaker holds back when the heart beats on its own. Seen in AAI mode or as the atrial part of a dual-chamber (DDD) pacemaker.
simulation_parameters: P-wave behavior: Spike about 0.04-0.05 s before each P wave
Other: Spike is narrow and about 0.5 mV tall.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: None when the device works. If it fails: dizziness, fatigue, syncope, palpitations. Pacemaker syndrome can occur with loss of AV synchrony.
pathologies.diagnosis: Spike before every P wave. Verify capture (spike followed by P), sensing (no spike on native beats) and rate. Confirm with device interrogation.
pathologies.treatment: None if functioning. If the device fails to capture, sense or pace: check leads, battery and output settings, and contact the device clinic or cardiology. For symptomatic bradycardia: transcutaneous pacing and standard bradycardia measures (atropine may help if SA node function remains).
pathologies.recommendations: Carry a pacemaker ID card. Follow MRI safety rules. Avoid strong magnets and check the generator pocket. Keep regular device interrogations. Teach the patient to check their pulse.
key_learning_points: A tiny vertical spike comes right before every P wave; the QRS stays narrow.
Check capture (spike then P), sensing (no spike on native beats) and rate.
No treatment if it works: troubleshoot only failures.
sources: 1. Parkes C. EKG Interpretation, part 11: Artificial Pacemakers, Tachycardia and Bradycardia. LevelUpRN. leveluprn.com/blogs/ekg-interpretation/11-artificial-pacemakers-tachycardia-bradycardia
2. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.

required.explanation: A pacing spike precedes atrial depolarization.
Each atrial pacing spike captures a P wave in the teaching pattern.

supporting.explanation: P wave morphology is paced rather than sinus.
Paced rhythm is typically regular.
Native AV conduction produces a measurable PR.
QRS is usually narrow with native ventricular conduction.

conflicts.explanation: Ventricular spikes favor ventricular pacing.
No pacing spike conflicts with a paced rhythm.

pathologies.definition: A rhythm driven by an artificial pacemaker that stimulates the ventricle. A pacing spike is followed by a wide QRS (usually with a left bundle branch block pattern), because the impulse starts in the ventricle and not in the normal conduction system.
ecg_characteristics: Heart rate: Set by the pacemaker (lower rate usually 60-80 bpm)
Rhythm: Regular
P wave: Absent, or dissociated and unrelated to the QRS
PR interval: Not applicable
QRS complex: Wide (more than 0.12 s), preceded by a spike
R-R interval: Regular
ST segment: Discordant (secondary changes)

Other relevant characteristics: Capture means every spike is followed by a QRS. Failure to capture is a spike with no QRS. Failure to sense is a spike that appears after a native beat. Oversensing shows as pauses without spikes.
simulation_parameters: QRS duration: 0.14-0.18 s, mostly negative in lead II
Other: Spike about 0.09 s before the QRS; discordant T wave.
pathologies.clinical_signs_symptoms: None when working. Failure: dizziness, syncope, bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue. Pacemaker syndrome (loss of AV synchrony): fatigue, neck pulsations, low blood pressure.
pathologies.diagnosis: Spike followed by a wide QRS. Check capture, sensing and rate. Spike without QRS: failure to capture (lead dislodgement, battery, high threshold from hyperkalemia, MI or drugs). Spikes at the wrong time: undersensing. No spikes when needed: oversensing or battery failure. Confirm a pulse for every QRS. Use device interrogation and a chest X-ray for lead position.
pathologies.treatment: Capturing and perfusing: no treatment. Failure: check connections and battery, increase output, reposition leads; transcutaneous pacing as a bridge; atropine, dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min per the bradycardia algorithm; treat hyperkalemia; urgent cardiology or electrophysiology. A magnet can force asynchronous pacing temporarily. If there is a QRS after each spike but no pulse, it is PEA: start CPR.
pathologies.recommendations: When using a defibrillator, place pads at least 8 cm (3 in) from the generator. Carry a device ID card. Keep MRI safety rules and follow-up interrogations.
key_learning_points: A spike followed by a wide QRS; each spike should capture a QRS.
Spike with no QRS is failure to capture; missing spikes when needed suggests failure to sense or oversensing.
Always check for a pulse: electrical capture does not guarantee mechanical capture.
sources: 1. Kusumoto FM, et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay. Circulation. 2019;140(8):e382-e482.
2. Panchal AR, et al. Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2):S366-S468.

required.explanation: A pacing spike precedes ventricular depolarization.
Each ventricular pacing spike captures a QRS in the teaching pattern.

supporting.explanation: Ventricular pacing produces a wide QRS.
Paced ventricular rhythm is usually regular.
P waves may be absent or unrelated to paced QRS.
PR is not applicable to ventricular pacing.

conflicts.explanation: Atrial-only spikes favor atrial pacing.
No pacing spike conflicts with a paced rhythm.

classifier_schema.purpose: Educational rule-based ECG rhythm pattern matching for ECGenius Predict. Not a clinical diagnostic tool.

inputs.label: Heart Rate
inputs.ui_hint: Use a numeric bpm when measurable; choose Unmeasurable for chaotic rhythms such as VF.

inputs.label: Pause Behavior
inputs.show_when: A pause or dropped-beat pattern is present or suspected.

inputs.label: Atrial:Ventricular Conduction Ratio
inputs.show_when: Flutter or AV block is suspected, or more P waves than QRS complexes are visible.

rule_types.required: A defining feature. If answered and contradicted, the rhythm is excluded. If unanswered/unclear, the result may remain possible but should not be labeled a strong match.
rule_types.supporting: Adds weighted evidence when matched. A missing/unclear value adds no score.
rule_types.conflict: Subtracts/excludes when a clearly contradictory feature is present.

scoring.strong_match_guidance: All answered required rules must match and the normalized supporting match should be high relative to alternatives.
scoring.ambiguity_guidance: If the top two compatible rhythms have close normalized scores or key differentiating required fields are unknown, return an ambiguous result with both candidates.
scoring.insufficient_guidance: If too few discriminating inputs are known, or no rhythm satisfies its required rules, request more/reviewed information.

classifier_schema.safety_copy: ECGenius compares entered characteristics with educational ECG rhythm patterns. It does not analyze a clinical ECG and does not provide a medical diagnosis.
